sections.h2: Where do you record a deed in Yuma County?
sections.html:
Deeds go to the Yuma County Recorder's Office at 298 S. Main Street, Yuma, AZ 85364. The county's Recorder page flags this as a new address, and the office is next to a pizza shop on that block. Counter hours are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, and the phone is (928) 373-6020.

The Recorder creates and maintains the county's public records and also runs voter registration and early voting, so the same office handles both jobs. Some older county pages still show a different street number for the Recorder. Use 298 S. Main Street and call ahead if you plan to drop off a signed deed on closing day.

Deeds are not filed at the Assessor or Treasurer. Those two offices share the building at 197 S. Main Street. The Assessor handles parcel values and ownership records, and the Treasurer bills and collects the tax.

sections.h2: What are your options for recording a document in Yuma County?
sections.html:
The county lists three routes: in person, by mail and electronically. Which one you use depends mostly on who is closing the sale. Title and escrow companies normally record electronically, while individual owners often bring the paper deed to the counter.

MethodWhat the Recorder lists
In person298 South Main Street, Yuma, AZ 85364, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. weekdays
By mailAttention: Recording Division, same street address, check or money order payable to Yuma County Recorder
ElectronicThrough third-party providers: Data Services, Inc., eRecording Partners Network, Indecomm Global Services, CSC eRecording and Simplifile

Source: Yuma County Recorder, How to Record a Document. For electronic recording, contact one of the providers directly. For a mailed document, ask the office at (928) 373-6020 for the current recording fee and what to include with the package.

sections.h2: What has to accompany a deed in Yuma County?
sections.html:
A deed that transfers title needs an affidavit, and A.R.S. 11-1133 spells out the rule. Buyer and seller, or an agent for either, certify the details on a Department of Revenue form, and the recorder has to refuse a deed that lacks a complete affidavit unless it is marked as exempt.

The affidavit asks for details that the Assessor later uses to update the parcel:

  • the buyer and seller names, addresses and phone numbers, and where to send the tax statement
  • the legal description, street address and assessor's parcel number
  • the sale date, the total consideration, the cash down payment and the type of financing
  • the relationship between the parties, if any, and whether the home will be owner-occupied or rented

A.R.S. 11-1134 exempts transfers such as deeds of gift, court-ordered conveyances, no-money quitclaims, confirmation or correction deeds, transfers to create joint tenancy with right of survivorship, and trustee's deeds under a deed of trust. The instrument must name the exemption it claims. The Recorder's FAQ list includes both "What is an Affidavit of Real Property Value?" and "What is an Exemption Code?", so ask the office if the form confuses you.

sections.h2: What questions does the Yuma County Recorder answer?
sections.html:
The county's recorder FAQ lists 23 questions. Several matter to someone selling a house, and the office is the place to ask about any of them.

  • How to find out whether a property has liens, and how to get a copy of a deed
  • How to add or remove a name on a property, and how to add or remove property from a trust
  • How to change ownership of a piece of property
  • What a declaration of homestead is
  • How to learn about a house in foreclosure
  • What the requirements for recording are, and the most common reasons documents are rejected
  • How to get a copy of a marriage license or a divorce decree, and whether the office can tell you a property's sale price
  • Whether the office offers notary service

The Assessor's FAQ adds that a copy of a deed comes from the Recorder, that the Assessor's online records show owners and sale prices, and that a manufactured home or recreational vehicle not affixed to real property is retitled at the Motor Vehicle Division, 2165 E. Gila Ridge Road, Yuma 85365, not at the county.

sections.h2: What taxes and liens affect a Yuma County sale?
sections.html:
Property tax rides along with the house until it is paid. A.R.S. 42-17153 makes the tax a lien that attaches on January 1 of the tax year and ranks ahead of other liens and encumbrances, except state liens and liens for taxes of other years. Your title company will order a payoff figure from the Treasurer before it records the deed.

The Treasurer's calendar shows 2026 first-half taxes were due October 1 and became delinquent after 5:00 p.m. on November 2, 2026, a date that has passed. The second half is due March 1, 2027 and delinquent after May 3, 2027. A 5 percent penalty applies on January 1, 2027 to delinquent 2025 taxes, and the lien sale for those years is February 18, 2027, with payment due by 5:00 p.m. on February 17 to avoid it.

Call the Treasurer at (928) 539-7781 for a balance. If you want to confirm how the county classified your home, the Assessor's Notice of Value explains the code for owner-occupied residences and rentals.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Yuma County itself?
sections.html:
Yuma County fills the southwestern corner of Arizona, with an area of 5,519 square miles. It borders California across the Colorado River and the Mexican state of Sonora to the south, and the lowest point in Arizona is on the river at San Luis. The 2020 census counted 203,881 people, and the county seat is the city of Yuma.

The county's own pages list the incorporated places as the City of Yuma, the City of San Luis, the City of Somerton and the Town of Wellton, plus the community of Dateland. The county was one of four original Arizona counties, created by the first territorial legislature, and lost its northern half when La Paz County was formed in 1982.

Yuma County government publishes recorder forms and a recorded-documents search through the Recorder's menu. Owner names, parcel numbers and sale data are on the Assessor's online records site at yumacountyaz-assessor.tylerhost.net/assessor/web, which is the quickest way to confirm a parcel number before you fill out the affidavit.

faqs.q: Where is the Yuma County Recorder's office?
faqs.a: The office is at 298 S. Main Street, Yuma, AZ 85364, and the county calls it a new address. Hours are 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, and the phone number is (928) 373-6020. Mailed documents go to Attention: Recording Division at the same address.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed electronically in Yuma County?
faqs.a: Yes, through third-party providers. The county names Data Services, Inc., eRecording Partners Network, Indecomm Global Services, CSC eRecording and Simplifile. Contact one of them directly, since the Recorder's page lists them as the e-recording options rather than a county portal.

faqs.q: How much does Yuma County charge to record a deed?
faqs.a: Ask the Recorder's Office at (928) 373-6020 for the current amount before you mail anything. For mailed documents, the county asks for a check or money order payable to Yuma County Recorder. Your title company will include the recording charge on the closing statement.

faqs.q: Does a Yuma County deed need an affidavit of property value?
faqs.a: Usually yes. A.R.S. 11-1133 requires an affidavit of legal value with each deed that transfers title, and the recorder must refuse an incomplete one. A.R.S. 11-1134 lists exempt transfers, and the deed must state the exemption claimed.

faqs.q: How do I get a copy of my Yuma County deed?
faqs.a: Request it from the Yuma County Recorder's Office. The Assessor's FAQ directs deed copy requests to the Recorder, and the Recorder's FAQ has an entry on how to obtain a copy of your deed. Call (928) 373-6020 to ask about the request process and any copy charge.
